newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka says can avoid power crisis in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka says can avoid power crisis in 1997.

text.p: Sri Lanka's state power utility said on Thursday it could supply uninterrupted power through 1997 despite the absence of the northeast monsoon for the second straight year.

"We're confident that with new thermal power plants coming onstream we can ride out a possible drought and avoid power cuts which dislocated commerce and industry last year," Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) chairman Arjun Deraniyagala said.
"The northeast monsoon which should have broken by the end of 1996 has failed," he told a news conference. "We have taken action to supply uninterrupted power throughout the year."
The island endured daily power cuts of up to eight hours at the height of the drought last year.

Water levels in hydropower reservoirs, which supply 85 percent of the country's electricity, plunged to dangerously low levels with the failure of the northeast monsoon and the delayed onset of the southwest monsoon.
Deraniyagala said the CEB had based its thermal power needs on very conservative rainfall estimates for 1997.

"The northeast monsoon which should have topped up our reservoirs at the end of last year was not enough," he said. "But because of the corrective steps we have taken, the water storage is better than in early 1996."

Current water levels in hydropower reservoirs were enough to generate 800 million units of electricty compared to the 600 million units of storage capacity available at the begining of 1996, Deraniyagala said.
The island has an installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power, he said.

Deraniyagala also said the CEB had no immediate plans to raise electricity tariffs for consumers but could be forced to do so later on if the huge cost of increased thermal power generation proved too much for the utility to bear.

"We feel confident that as things are the consumer need not be inconvenienced in any way," he said. "But consumers should also conserve power as much as possible because in future we'll have to depend more on thermal power which is extremely expensive."
The CEB planned to reduce its dependence on hydropower by building more thermal power plants, Deraniyagala said.

Sri Lanka will generate 1,050 million units of electricity, or 43 percent of its needs, from thermal sources by the end of the first half of 1997, reducing the share of hydropower to 1,400 million units, or 57 percent of the requirement, he said.
Under emergency power generation measures the CEB will hire 83 megawatts providing 275 million units from small private sector diesel plants, he added.
A 20 megawatt plant has been connected to a system providing about 38 million units while a 40 megawatt plant, providing 90 million units, will be connected by April, Deraniyagala said.
